documents.abstract: Under the background of digital transformation in the construction industry, Building Information Modeling (BIM) and artificial intelligence (AI) have become an important technical path to promote the intelligent upgrading of the construction industry. AI-BIM integration improves design efficiency, project control quality and building full lifecycle management capability. Fragmented data and poor interoperability hinder its widespread use. This paper conducts a literature review to summarise AI-BIM applications in automated design, construction management, operation and maintenance optimisation, and cross-stage collaboration. This paper further looks into how key technologies like machine learning, computer vision and NLP can be integrated. It also sums up current challenges and future research directions. Studies show that AI can improve BIM's ability in data processing, scheme design and smart decision-making. In the future, combining AI with digital twins and large language models will break existing limits and support the high-quality development of intelligent construction.

Large language models (LLMs) and related conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems have moved rapidly from novelty into ordinary use across education, work, social life, and mental-health-related help seeking. Members of the public now use these systems for advice, companionship, self-disclosure, emotional support, psychoeducation, and quasi-therapeutic interactions. Existing instruments assess problematic or dependent AI use, but they do not ask whether AI has entered a pathway toward serious harm by entrenching ideation, operationalizing capability, displacing human support, or amplifying harmful conduct. To our knowledge, no brief, clinically oriented psychiatric screener has yet been developed and validated specifically for this purpose. We define dangerous AI use as generative AI use that appears to increase the likelihood, feasibility, persistence, organization, or scale of serious harm to self or others. This paper describes LLMs as interactive capability amplifiers and quasi-social systems rather than informational technologies alone, situates their risk within the technical problems of alignment and behavioral stability, and proposes a four-dimensional clinical formulation: Ideational Entrenchment, Operationalized Capability, Relational Displacement, and Broader Amplification. We then introduce two candidate instruments awaiting formal validation: the STEPS-5, a brief screen for AI involvement in acute self-harm and suicide risk, and the HEAT-4, a research-oriented framework addressing broader harmful-use amplification. These tools are intended to open clinical inquiry rather than diagnose, predict behavior, or determine disposition. Ultimately, we argue for the need to avoid both over-pathologizing ordinary AI use and ignoring when AI has become meaningfully relevant to psychiatric safety.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background The low prevalence and heterogeneous nature of rare diseases make them particularly difficult to diagnose and prognosticate. These issues are amplified in the paediatric population, who are disproportionately affected by rare diseases. Non-generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a powerful tool that can aid clinicians in diagnostics, risk stratification and patient subgrouping. The extent to which this has been applied to rare diseases, in particular paediatric rare disease cohorts, is not well defined. Objective This scoping review aimed to identify how AI techniques have been used to aid diagnosis and prognosis of rare diseases, with a focus on their use in paediatric populations. Methods Embase, Medline, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and Scopus databases were searched for original articles using the search terms “(‘machine learning’ OR ‘artificial intelligence’) AND (‘rare’ OR ‘orphan’) AND (‘condition*’ OR ‘disease*’ OR ‘disorder*’)”. Results One hundred and thirty-six studies met inclusion criteria, 28 (20.6%) of which used paediatric cohorts, with a variety of study types [diagnostic ( n = 61, 44.9%), prognostic ( n = 39, 28.7%), classification ( n = 19, 14.0%) and screening ( n = 17, 12.5%)]. The number of participants per study ranged from 16 to over 3 million. Tree-based models were the most frequently used in the studies ( n = 62, 45.6%) followed by neural networks ( n = 49, 36.1%) and linear models ( n = 46, 33.9%); the most frequent methods used in paediatric cohorts were neural networks ( n = 11, 39.2%), tree-based ( n = 10, 35.7%), and linear ( n = 10, 35.7%) models. Pre-processing steps were only described in a small number of studies, including feature selection ( n = 41, 30.1%), handling data missingness ( n = 36, 19.1%), data cleaning ( n = 44, 32.4%), addressing data imbalance ( n = 21, 15.4%), and data augmentation ( n = 23, 16.9%). Only 27 (19.9%) models were externally validated. Clinician involvement was described in 56 studies (41.2%), and no models had been translated into regular use in clinical practice. Conclusions AI tools to aid diagnosis and prognosis in rare diseases are increasingly being investigated, but their use for paediatric rare disease cohorts remains scarce. Limited methodological description of model development, clinician involvement and lack of external validation means there has been poor translation of models into clinical practice.

documents.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems extend large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge through a multi-stage pipeline. While this architecture can improve the factual grounding of generated answers, it introduces structural attack surfaces that extend beyond those of standalone LLMs. In this paper, we introduce a security meta-model that captures explicit causal relationships between RAG surfaces, attacks, weaknesses, risks, and CIA impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Its purpose is to provide security engineers with a structured and user-friendly framework for gathering and assessing the risks, weaknesses, and mitigations relevant to their RAG deployment. We designed the meta-model through an iterative, structured analysis of 43~publications (2023--2026) and instantiated it as a catalog populated with the security threats and remediations reported in the literature. Filtering the catalog according to a deployment configuration produces a risk profile containing the risks applicable to that deployment. An interactive web visualizer lets users navigate the catalog as a graph, follow causal chains, and explore stakeholder-specific views. Analysis of the catalog revealed a persistent imbalance between attack-focused and defense-focused research, a concentration of threats at ingestion, and coverage gaps affecting output integrity. Coverage is assessed against the OWASP LLM Top~10, and operational applicability is illustrated across textual, graph-based, and multimodal RAG configurations.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Green Finance have emerged as two of the most important forces that have the potential to drive the world towards a sustainable economy. The current paper attempts to explore the role of AI and Green Finance in promoting and supporting a sustainable economy with reference to building a Viksit Bharat 2047. A survey was conducted among 160 respondents, with the results analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation, regression, and an independent-samples t-test. The results demonstrated that the population studied had a generally positive perception about how AI can support Green Finance and lead the economy towards sustainability. The analysis identified strong awareness about AI as the biggest predictor of increased perception of the integration of AI and Green Finance (r = 0.78, p < .001). Additionally, participants who were aware of Green Finance had significantly higher scores for the perceived level of integration than those who were not (t = 2.65, p = .009). As such, there is reason to reject the null hypothesis, which claimed that there is no connection between the two concepts. Finally, the paper provides recommendations that financial institutions, regulators, and educators can consider in order to promote and support responsible and AI-enabled Green Finance.

This study explores the level of awareness and key influencing factors related to the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools among undergraduates in Sri Lanka’s state universities. As AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Google Gemini become increasingly prevalent in higher education, understanding how students perceive and adopt these technologies is critical. The study applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and the Technology Readiness Index (TRI) to examine four independent variables: Attitude, Peer Influence, Perceived Usefulness, and Technological Readiness. Data were collected from a sample of 384 undergraduates across state universities using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SPSS. Findings reveal that technological readiness and perceived usefulness are the strongest predictors of awareness, while gaps remain in ethical understanding. The study recommends integrating AI literacy and ethical guidelines into curricula to ensure responsible use. These findings provide practical guidance for policymakers and educators in developing strategies to enhance AI awareness and readiness among undergraduates.

The environmental comfort in university classrooms affects learners' cognitive efficiency and physical/mental state however most evaluations are restricted by comparing single physical parameter threshold without considering the mechanisms of human factors. From the perspective of human factors engineering this research includes three aspects such as theoretical construction, model design and mechanism analysis. Based on the integration of sensory thresholds, cognitive load and environmental stress theories, we established a progressive analytical framework and analyzed the interactive coupling characteristics between four types of environmental factors; developed a three-level tree-structured evaluation index system and a fuzzy preference weight aggregation strategy which can be used to construct a comprehensive evaluation mechanism that integrates both objective data-driven and subjective correction; Analyzing the pathway of factor transmissions via the stimulus-organism-response paradigm revealed the dynamic shaping effect of climate adaptation and behavior patterns on comfort needs so as to provide systematic theoretical tools and methodological supports for evaluating university classroom environment.

Purpose This study aims to examine current evidence on the educational use of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated video (AIGV) through a SWOT analysis and to outline plausible future scenarios for its adoption. Design/methodology/approach Relevant studies were identified through a structured literature search, and their findings were organized into strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Findings The analysis reveals that AIGV offers strengths, including rapid and efficient video production, accessibility and scalability, vivid visual storytelling and short-term learning outcomes comparable to human-made videos. However, key weaknesses include misinformation and content inaccuracies, limited teaching and social presence and blurred boundaries between authentic and synthetic content. Opportunities include multilingual delivery, personalized and adaptive learning, reflective learning through AI-generated scenarios and growing interest in AIGV across educational fields. Threats include ethical concerns related to autonomy, privacy and copyright; risks of biased representations; and trust and governance challenges limiting adoption. Research limitations/implications This study highlights the need for further research on how educators and institutions perceive and respond to the proposed future scenarios for AIGV adoption. Practical implications The findings can inform educators and institutions in making responsible decisions about the adoption of AIGV in education. Originality/value This paper contributes to the emerging literature on AIGV in education by applying a SWOT lens to synthesize current evidence and outline plausible future scenarios for its adoption.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In the artificial intelligence (AI) era, the structure of safety hazards in university laboratories is changing, with unconventional hazards making up a growing share. As AI evolves from an auxiliary tool into an autonomous research collaborator, interdisciplinary experiments are becoming faster and more intense, producing hazards that are more dynamic, less predictable, and harder to assess and prevent. Most laboratory safety frameworks, however, still rely on static rules built for known risks, and these are poorly suited to such emerging threats. A shift from static rule-based control toward dynamic risk management is therefore needed. Adopting a conceptual mapping approach rather than an empirical study, this paper examines how Zero Trust—a cybersecurity framework based on continuous trust evaluation—could be adapted to university laboratory safety. It defines three adapted attributes (universal distrust with dynamic verification, least privilege with dynamic adjustment, and continuous monitoring with real-time early warning), identifies the main implementation barriers, and suggests targeted responses.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming professional practices across library and information environments. This study aimed to identify the factors influencing the adoption of AI for librarians’ continuing professional development (CPD) through a systematic literature review (SLR) methodology. A total of 30 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from major global digital databases were systematically analyzed to synthesize the existing body of knowledge on AI adoption in librarianship. The findings revealed that attitudinal readiness, competency transformation, organizational readiness, experiential learning opportunities, and future-oriented professional identity significantly encourage the adoption of AI for librarians’ CPD. Conversely, insufficient structured CPD opportunities, resistance to technological change, limited technological infrastructure, and ethical concerns emerged as major barriers hindering effective AI integration in professional learning environments. Based on the findings, the study developed a comprehensive framework to support the efficient and sustainable adoption of AI for librarians’ CPD. The study contributes to the growing discourse on AI-enabled professional learning in library and information science by offering theoretical, practical, and strategic insights to enhance librarians’ readiness for AI-driven information environments.

This study examined the effect of advanced technology on shareholders’ value creation in Zenith Bank ltd and Wema Bank ltd with desire whether the adoption of AI, big data analytics and cloud computing impacts on shareholders' value creation. The study adopts survey research design using structured questionnaires to gather responds from the employees of the selected banks. Descriptive statistics and multiple regression analysis were used to analyse the data collected. The study's results showed that artificial intelligence and big data analytics positively impacted shareholders' value creation, likewise, cloud computing has significant and positive impact on shareholders' value creation. It is recommended that effective use of advanced technology improve operational efficiency, decision making and reduced operational expenditure therefore, management of banks should continuously invest in technological infrastructure and enhance employees' technological skills as technology-driven strategies.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, poses substantial challenges for early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring—two cornerstones of effective clinical management and therapeutic intervention. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), owing to its non-invasiveness and high spatial resolution, has emerged as an indispensable tool in AD research. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) techniques, has demonstrated remarkable potential for automating MRI analysis, extracting subtle imaging features, and supporting objective disease prediction. This review comprehensively summarizes the latest advances in AI-driven MRI applications for AD diagnosis, staging, prognosis, and adjuvant therapeutic monitoring. It highlights key progress in AI model development, multimodal data processing, and clinical translational value. Furthermore, current bottlenecks, including data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and real-world deployment, are systematically discussed, and future directions are outlined to enhance the precision and clinical utility of AI-assisted MRI in AD. Overall, AI-MRI has evolved from laboratory validation toward early clinical adoption, with explainability and multi-center generalizability identified as critical priorities in the next research phase.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid proliferation of 5G networks has enabled a wide range of data-intensive applications, including video streaming, online gaming, metaverse platforms, and real-time communication services. Understanding the behavior and characteristics of such heterogeneous traffic is essential for efficient network management, resource allocation, and quality of service (QoS) optimization. However, most existing studies rely on simulated or synthetic datasets, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive data-driven analysis of 5G traffic using a large-scale real-world dataset collected from commercial mobile networks. The dataset consists of over 328 h of traffic captured from diverse applications, including Netflix, YouTube Live, Zoom, Roblox, and cloud gaming platforms, using mobile-based packet capture tools without specialized hardware. The collected data is processed into a time-series format with packet-level features, enabling detailed traffic characterization and analysis. We investigate the effectiveness of machine learning and large language models (LLMs) in classifying and analyzing 5G traffic patterns across multiple application categories. Experimental results reveal that traditional structured machine learning approaches outperform LLM-based models in handling network traffic classification tasks, particularly in multi-class and imbalanced scenarios. Furthermore, LLM-based methods exhibit high rates of inconsistency and prediction bias, highlighting their limitations when applied to structured network data. The findings of this study provide practical insights into the suitability of different AI approaches for real-world 5G traffic analysis. The proposed framework contributes to the development of more reliable and efficient traffic classification systems, supporting advanced network optimization, intelligent traffic management, and future 5G/6G deployments.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning is now very familiar also used in many applications. This is mainly used to monitor the decision done by own system compared to previous methods. Nowadays this system used in many applications like networking, healthcare and etc. But sometimes it may give some worrying to the people about their safety. Even though ML models usually do well predicting things, they can still get tricked by something called adversarial attacks inputs designed to make the model fail and give wrong answers. To help users understand why an AI made a certain decision and boost confidence in these systems, researchers turned to XAI. We look at ways attackers get in, how explanations work, security weak spots, and what defenses we have. It introduces a Robust Explainability Framework (REF) that spots threats, tests explanations, checks robustness, and adds human supervision. This is all to create models that aren't just right but also secure, clear, and dependable fit for serious use in the real world.

AEGIS NEXUS AI is an intelligent AI-driven business planning and decision-support system designed to assist entrepreneurs in planning and designing business spaces. The system leverages Generative AI, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to analyze business type, space dimensions, requirements, budget, and purchasing preferences. Developed using Python, FastAPI, React, Machine Learning, LLMs, RAG, and vector databases, the system provides personalized recommendations for furniture, equipment, machinery, estimated costs, and retail or wholesale purchasing options. It can also generate conceptual floor-plan layouts based on user-provided dimensions and requirements. With its integration of Generative AI, RAG, intelligent recommendations, and space planning, AEGIS NEXUS AI simplifies business planning and supports informed decisions on space utilization, resource selection, and estimated investment.

Physics-based simulation underpins engineering analysis but remains difficult to deploy in practice due to complex setup, parameterization, and interpretation. While large language model-based agentic systems have shown promise in automating engineering computing workflows, they have primarily targeted structured, mesh-based problems. We present the first agentic AI workflow for meshless simulation in computational mechanics, demonstrated on debris flow modeling using Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) with the software DualSPHysics. By integrating tool orchestration, multimodal inputs (text and hand-sketches), and human-in-the-loop interaction, the framework enables end-to-end simulation workflows for a class of problems that are inherently less structured and more challenging to automate. Results show that multimodal inputs not only enhance user experience but also reduce failure modes over text-only descriptions. Human-in-the-loop is critical for resolving ambiguities and handling SPH-specific configurations. We further introduce a cognitive-task-based evaluation for post-processing that suggests, for each aspect of performance, whether improvement should come from clearer prompts, domain skills, or more capable LLMs. These results establish the viability of agentic AI for particle-based simulation and underscore its potential to transform the accessibility and efficiency of computational mechanics workflows.

This study examined artificial intelligence algorithm fairness and bias in academic library information systems at Ramat Library, University of Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey design was used. The study involved 152 library professionals and 385 library users. Data were collected using structured questionnaires assessing AI-driven service implementation, awareness of algorithmic bias, user perceptions, and institutional gaps. Descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation, and an independent-samples t-test were used for analysis. AI-driven service implementation was moderate (mean = 2.62, SD = 0.91), while awareness of algorithmic bias among library professionals was also moderate (mean = 2.59, SD = 0.87). Users generally perceived AI search results as fair, but reported weaker representation of local and Indigenous knowledge and multilingual materials. Institutional gaps were rated high (mean = 3.37, SD = 0.82), particularly the absence of an AI governance policy and bias-auditing protocols. A significant positive association was observed between AI service implementation and awareness of algorithmic bias (r = 0.387, p < 0.001), whereas no significant difference was found in bias perceptions by gender (t = 1.24, p = 0.216). The findings support the need for context-sensitive AI governance, staff capacity building, bias auditing, participatory oversight, and improved multilingual and Indigenous knowledge representation in academic library information systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of digital technologies and internet-based applications has significantly increased the risk of cyber threats, making software security a critical concern. Traditional security systems mainly rely on predefined rules and signature-based detection techniques, which often fail to identify new and sophisticated attacks. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an effective solution to overcome these limitations by providing intelligent, adaptive, and automated security mechanisms. AI-based security systems use technologies such as Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Behavioral Analysis to monitor software activities, detect anomalies, and identify potential threats in real time. These systems can analyze large volumes of data, recognize malicious patterns, and respond quickly to security incidents without extensive human intervention. AI also enhances malware detection, intrusion detection, user authentication, phishing prevention, and vulnerability assessment. This research paper examines the role of AI in strengthening software security by discussing its working principles, applications, advantages, challenges, and future opportunities. The study highlights how AI improves threat detection accuracy, reduces response time, and provides proactive protection against evolving cyberattacks. Despite challenges such as data dependency, privacy concerns, and implementation costs, AI-based security systems have the potential to revolutionize cybersecurity and create a more secure digital environment

ABSTRACT The rise of AI companions has sparked interest in their potential to alleviate the growing social problem of loneliness, yet evidence of their effectiveness remains unsettled. Drawing on social surrogacy theory with a theories‐in‐use approach, this research introduces synthetic mindfulness, defined as consumers' judgment of an AI companion's capacity to maintain an attentive presence, engage in a non‐judgmental way, and respond with sensitive attunement to their needs. We argue that these judgments shape whether consumers experience AI companions as capable of reducing their loneliness. Across one qualitative and four quantitative studies, we develop and validate a three‐dimensional measure of synthetic mindfulness. Our final study demonstrates that higher judgments of synthetic mindfulness reduce loneliness via consumers' strengthened sense of belonging and self‐esteem. This research advances understanding of how AI companions can effectively address loneliness and provides a conceptual foundation for examining synthetic mindfulness in human–AI relationships.

In the context of rapid digitalization and intelligent governance, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly embedded in organizational supervision and decision-making processes, fundamentally reshaping how supervisory boards process information and perform monitoring tasks. Drawing on information processing theory, this study develops a moderated mediation model to examine how AI empowerment is associated with supervisory board effectiveness through information transparency, and how this process is contingent upon organizational learning capability. Using survey data collected from 382 supervisory board members and senior managers across multiple industries, this study adopts an organizational-level perspective and employs hierarchical regression and bootstrap analyses to test the proposed hypotheses. The results show that AI empowerment significantly associated with both information transparency and supervisory board effectiveness. Information transparency partially mediates the relationship between AI empowerment and supervisory effectiveness, indicating that AI is positively associated with supervisory performance by optimizing organizational information-processing mechanisms. Moreover, organizational learning capability positively moderates the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency. However, the moderated mediation effect is not statistically significant, indicating that the indirect effect of AI empowerment on supervisory effectiveness through information transparency remains relatively stable across different levels of organizational learning capability. These findings suggest that organizational learning capability shapes the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency, but does not significantly alter the overall indirect pathway to supervisory effectiveness.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-generated information within justice systems has intensified questions concerning evidentiary reliability, authenticity, human oversight, and institutional accountability. As the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules prepares to revisit proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 and potential amendments to Rule 901 on October 15, 2026, the legal system is confronting how AI-generated evidence should be evaluated. However, a critical governance question remains insufficiently addressed: What happens after technology-generated information enters the human decision-making process? This paper examines the distinction between technical reliability, evidentiary admissibility, and human decision accountability. It introduces the Decision Visibility Gap, a condition in which institutions preserve technology outputs and resulting actions but lack sufficient evidence to reconstruct how human decision-makers received, interpreted, verified, relied upon, and acted on that information. Drawing upon scholarship concerning automation bias, algorithmic accountability, human oversight, and sociotechnical governance, the paper presents Justice Decision Observability (JDO), an independent governance and decision-evidence framework developed by Justice Beacon Solutions (JBS). Through hypothetical applications involving law enforcement, correctional operations, and community supervision, the analysis demonstrates how technically reliable outputs may coexist with incomplete human decision records. It further distinguishes evidence-centered governance from traditional technology audits, compliance assessments, and employee evaluations. The paper argues that establishing the reliability of AI-generated evidence does not independently establish the traceability, justification, or evidentiary completeness of the human decisions influenced by that evidence. Effective justice governance therefore requires attention not only to what technology produces, but also to how institutional authority is exercised around those outputs. Justice Decision Observability is presented as a conceptual and operational framework for making the human decision layer visible, explainable, and supported by evidence, while recognizing the need for further empirical validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As the leading cause of permanent vision loss worldwide, glaucoma poses a significant public health problem because it is a condition that progresses slowly and has highly complex multi-modal diagnostic needs. This paper offers a broad review of how Artificial Intelligence (AI) has developed through the clinical spectrum of glaucoma treatment, ranging from initial diagnosis and glaucoma severity, to now personalized treatment planning and surgical guidance. The AI models use deep learning architectures, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and multi-modal transformers, to automatically process intricate diagnostic data like color fundus photography, Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans, visual field perimetry, and Electronic Health Records (EHRs). In addition, predictive algorithms can enable personalized treatment based on the prediction of disease progression rates, intraocular pressure fluctuations and the selection of more appropriate surgical candidates. Although the advantages are clear, there are important obstacles to broader adoption in clinical practice, such as variations in hardware across different devices, risk of bias in the algorithms used by different patient populations, data privacy issues, and the 'black-box' nature of deep learning. Newly developed concepts such as the Explainable AI, the use of wearable sensors for continuous monitoring, and the use of genomic risk profiles are bridging these gaps. In the end, AI is an objective, rapid, clinical decision support tool to assist clinical practice, improve the efficiency of teleophthalmology screenings and protect the patient's visual function.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency with studies reporting relative performance gains of 20–35% in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to theorise how AI-driven acceleration reconfigures firms’ temporal assets, creating efficiency gains while destroying relational time (trust, loyalty, premium value), a hidden cost invisible to managerial accounting but acutely felt by customers. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-method dual-coding design combining qualitative coding of 2,000 reviews (from a 1.2 M Google Maps corpus across 10 luxury chains) with an automated Gemini natural language processing extraction. The comparative design developed temporal categories and validated brand-level friction patterns while proving human interpretation essential to detect Kairos deficits and distinguish intentional deceleration from service failure. Findings Systematic temporal fractures where AI acceleration destroys relational value. Five Strategic Temporal Archetypes (Decelerator, Bifurcator, Autonomy Provider, Fragmentor, Automator) represent distinct competitive positions on the efficiency-experience frontier. Research limitations/implications This study extends AI, service and organisational temporality research by conceptualising AI as a temporal agent and introducing Kairos deficit, temporal extraction and temporal co-destruction. It also demonstrates the value of dual-coding methodologies combining computational scale with qualitative interpretation. Future research should test Strategic Temporal Governance and its archetypes across sectors, cultures and longitudinally. Practical implications Organisations should move beyond efficiency metrics towards strategic temporal governance. AI deployment should distinguish contexts where Chronos optimisation creates value from those requiring Kairos, intentional pacing and relational attention. AI systems should incorporate temporal transparency and human override, while managers should recognise frontline resistance to acceleration as potentially valuable temporal mediation. Social implications AI-driven acceleration can reduce opportunities for reflection, relational engagement and meaningful participation. When organisational speed dominates, technological progress may privilege efficiency over human temporal needs. Recognising Kairos alongside Chronos therefore matters socially, helping preserve spaces for deliberation, care, relational attention and human override rather than assuming that faster interaction always represents social progress. Originality/value Introduces temporal reconfiguration and Kairos deficit as strategic constructs; develops qualitative coding and constant comparison for lived experience at scale; validates the qualitative–computational distinction through comparative dual-coding against automated LLM extraction; reframes AI implementation as competitive positioning, not operational optimisation.

The second national study, “Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index,” tracks changes in attitudes, knowledge, and practices regarding the use of AI in the Bulgarian public administration between 2025 and 2026. The data was collected from 5,475 employees at the central, regional, and municipal levels. In 2026, the overall Index score increased, with the administration remaining in the “capacity-building” phase. The most noticeable progress was in the practical use of AI and employees’ readiness to work with such tools. At the same time, the institutional environment is evolving more slowly. Limited access to approved tools, the lack of clear internal rules, and poor knowledge sharing continue to be major obstacles. The results show that the sustainable implementation of AI in public administration requires not only more skills and training, but also clear responsibilities, secure access, and mechanisms for institutional learning. The raw data from the study are available in the open research repository Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22026174.

This study assessed the levels of AI readiness, perceived utility, and professional integration of artificial intelligence among medical technologists in selected clinical and hospital laboratories in Cavite and examined the relationships among these variables. Grounded in a socio-technical perspective that integrates the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the research employed a descriptive-correlational design. One hundred licensed medical technologists were selected through purposive sampling according to predefined inclusion criteria. AI readiness was measured with the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students, perceived utility with the Professional Impact subscale of the Shinners Artificial Intelligence Perception questionnaire, and professional integration with items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Respondents demonstrated high levels of AI readiness (mean = 3.60) and perceived utility (mean = 3.64), indicating adequate knowledge, technical skills, and positive perceptions toward AI use in laboratory practice. Professional integration was also rated high (mean = 3.61), although AI remained only moderately embedded in routine workflows and many respondents were neutral regarding the actual extent of use. Correlation analyses revealed very weak, non-significant relationships among the three constructs, indicating that individual readiness and favorable perceptions did not translate into greater professional integration. The findings suggest that organizational and contextual factors—such as institutional support, infrastructure, and policy implementation—play a more decisive role in AI adoption than individual-level attributes alone. The study recommends structured, hands-on AI training programs tailored to laboratory practice, clear institutional policies and protocols for incorporating AI outputs into diagnostic workflows, and future research employing probability sampling, multi-regional samples, and longitudinal designs. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 3 by supporting improved diagnostic capacity and laboratory-enabled clinical decision-making, and to Sustainable Development Goal 9 by examining the conditions required for sustainable adoption of innovative health technologies. It advances public-health and institutional sustainability by clarifying the socio-technical determinants that enable resilient, digitally enabled laboratory services in resource-constrained settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly proposed as a way to extend feedback, practice, and learner support in online universities. This critical narrative review examines the replacement, partnership, and pedagogical-risk claims made for AI tutoring. It synthesises foundational evidence on intelligent tutoring systems, recent evaluations of generative-AI tutoring, research on teaching and social presence in online learning, and current educational-governance guidance. The evidence does not support a general claim that AI tutors can replace human tutors. Structured intelligent tutoring systems have often outperformed conventional instructional comparators, but results against individual human tutoring are mixed and depend on subject, comparison condition, outcome measure, and implementation. Recent generative-AI studies show promise in carefully engineered, bounded learning tasks; they do not establish effectiveness for generic chatbots or whole-programme substitution. A partnership model is therefore more defensible when it assigns AI bounded roles in practice, preliminary feedback, and pattern detection while retaining human accountability for pedagogical design, consequential decisions, exception handling, and community facilitation. The review positions ENGAGE—Engage, Navigate, Guide, Articulate, Gather, Evolve—as a design-and-governance framework that translates those principles into an iterative course-level cycle. It also distinguishes documented capability and governance concerns from broader claims that remain plausible but under-tested, including cognitive deskilling. For online-university leaders, the practical question is not whether to automate tutoring wholesale, but how to design, disclose, evaluate, and govern hybrid configurations that improve learning without displacing educational responsibility.

documents.abstract: THE INVARIANT SCRIPT AND THE STAGE : To the chief executives, venture capitalists, and algorithmic architects currently orchestrating the landscape of artificial intelligence: you are not the authors of the play; you are simply transient actors who have been handed a very loud microphone. On the contemporary stage of global capital, you wear the robes of a king. You command data centers that consume the energy of small nations, deploy models that alter human cognition, and witness financial valuations that mirror the GDP of empires. This unprecedented accumulation of wealth, physiological optimization, and political access creates a dangerous psychological feedback loop: the illusion of absolute autonomy. However, when the theatre curtains fall, the executive is stripped of the costume. In the sweeping scope of the cosmos, the most powerful tech leader remains a fragile, dependent speck of life—breathing air they did not engineer, occupying a body they cannot permanently preserve, and standing completely subservient to the ultimate power of the universe. On the stage you are a king, but in reality, you are a small human being.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for qualitative analysis in substance use research, yet their performance relative to human coders remains underexplored. This study compares ChatGPT-4.0 with human coders in performing qualitative coding tasks using NIH grant abstracts as a test case, focusing on the identification and description of research innovations. Using a sample of NIH HEAL Initiative grant abstracts related to opioid overdose prevention, a total of 125 abstracts were independently coded by ChatGPT and humans to generate innovation descriptions, which were then evaluated by both human raters and ChatGPT for depth/detail and relevance/completeness using 5-point Likert scales. Identical instructions were used across all coding and evaluation stages. ChatGPT-generated descriptions were consistently rated higher than human-generated descriptions on both dimensions. Human evaluators rated ChatGPT outputs at an average of 4.47 for both depth/detail and relevance/completeness, compared to 3.33 and 3.24 for human outputs, respectively (F(1,176)=133.9, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that LLMs, when carefully prompted, can enhance the efficiency and quality of qualitative research evaluation.

Abstract Previous work built AI-based surrogates for a nonlinear gyrokinetic simulation code with the goal of using them for fast, direct calculations of turbulent ion heat flux in stellarator design optimizations and scenario planning for experiments. These AI surrogates were trained on data from \textgreater{}200k nonlinear, adiabatic electron gyrokinetic simulations with the gyrokinetic flux-tube code GX, using a wide range of stellarator magnetic configurations ($\sim$23k), positions in the plasma, and gradient scale lengths. In this paper, we demonstrate the use of the AI-based turbulence surrogate in the optimization of stellarator magnetic equilibrium and to speed up stellarator transport solvers. Due to its speed ($\sim${}ms), the AI-based surrogate enables previously unattainable optimization objectives, such as full radial profiles of ion turbulent heat flux, or directly optimizing to maximize the turbulent critical gradient at multiple locations across the plasma. These direct calculations provide a potentially more accurate optimization target and reduce reliance on ad-hoc heuristics that may not accurately capture the variation of turbulent transport with magnetic configuration. By including the AI-based surrogate for turbulent heat flux in a transport solver, we can quickly postprocess and confirm the improved ion temperature resulting from the optimized equilibrium. Finally, we demonstrate the use of AI agents with strong reasoning AI models to automate the outer loop, exploring many objective and hyperparameter configurations with this AI-based turbulence surrogate to discover improved turbulence optimized magnetic equilibria.

BACKGROUND: Carotid ultrasound is traditionally confined to specialist settings because examination quality and diagnostic reliability are highly dependent on the operator's technical skill and experience. Recent advances in AI-assisted ultrasound may enable task shifting to primary care staff and support the integration of personalized visual risk communication into routine preventive care. Visualization of subclinical atherosclerosis has been shown to strengthen cardiovascular risk communication and support preventive engagement. However, limited evidence exists on how such technology can be practically integrated into routine primary care workflows and what conditions are required to support use by nonexpert operators. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to describe an iterative user-centered design process enabling nonexpert use of AI-assisted carotid ultrasound for visualizing subclinical atherosclerosis in primary care cardiovascular disease prevention. METHODS: We conducted a user-centered, iterative study within the Västerbotten Intervention Programme in northern Sweden. Fourteen nurse assistants from 4 primary care centers representing urban, rural, and remote rural settings tested an AI-assisted carotid ultrasound prototype with real-time guidance and artery segmentation in their primary care work environment, while 15 nurse assistants participated in semistructured interviews. Structured system-interaction observations were conducted during prototype testing. Interview data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's approach, while data from structured system-interaction observations were analyzed pragmatically to identify usability and workflow issues relevant to the iterative development process. RESULTS: The thematic analysis of interview data identified 4 themes describing nurse assistants' experiences and conditions for implementation: technology that fits the everyday primary care work; system guidance as a prerequisite for effective use; practical, peer-supported learning for confidence in clinical use; and confidence in the patient encounter. Observations identified recurring usability challenges related to ergonomics, probe handling, interface navigation, image acquisition, and time pressure. These findings led to iterative refinements, including redesigned interface navigation, simplified data entry, added audio feedback, enhanced probe support, and revised training materials. CONCLUSIONS: This user-centered study identified key practical, organizational, and educational conditions for integrating AI-assisted carotid ultrasound into routine preventive care by nonexpert staff in primary care. The findings suggest that successful implementation will depend not only on technical capability but also on ergonomic and workflow fit, intuitive system guidance, peer-supported learning, and confidence in patient communication. These findings provide a foundation for future validation and implementation studies.

documents.abstract: This record presents Version 0.9.0 of an open, non-peer-reviewed research artifact documenting the substantial use of an AI agent across an end-to-end educational research workflow. OpenAI Codex contributed to research-question generation, variable feasibility assessment, analysis planning, R and Python code generation, execution support, literature synthesis, manuscript drafting, validation, revision, and reproducibility documentation. The human researcher defined the overall objective, selected the research domain, directed the use of open R/Python methods, approved major workflow gates, requested sensitivity analyses and corrections, questioned the comparability of scores across TIMSS cycles, and authorized this public release. The AI system is not an author. Independent human verification of every analytical and interpretive claim has not been completed. The empirical workflow used Korean Grade 8 student data from TIMSS 2015 and TIMSS 2023. The recorded analytical environment used R 4.4.3 and Python 3.12.13, with random seed 20260802. Methods included weighted Gaussian latent profile analysis, TIMSS JK2 variance estimation, five mathematics plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules, BCH-type three-step correction, simulation and unit testing, sensitivity analyses, and an independent JK2 cross-check using the R survey package version 4.5. No commercial statistical software was required. A subsequent audit of official TIMSS documentation identified a critical measurement limitation. The 2023 metrics for Students Like Learning Mathematics (BSBGSLM) and Students Confident in Mathematics (BSBGSCM) were reset in 2023. Their 2015 and 2023 numerical scores are therefore not directly comparable. The Students Value Mathematics scale (BSBGSVM) retained the 2011 trend metric. Consequently, the cross-cycle profile means, shapes, and proportions reported in the included manuscript must not be interpreted as changes on a common 2015–2023 attitude scale. Item-level linking and multigroup measurement-invariance analysis are required before making such claims. The deposit includes the AI-generated manuscript, a Korean paper-development record, research-question materials, three sets of AI-agent instructions and prompts, R and Python code, aggregate analytical outputs, tables, figures, validation reports, failed-analysis records, approval and decision logs, software-environment information, file manifests, SHA-256 checksums, licensing information, and reproduction instructions. TIMSS student-level source files and row-level derived data are not redistributed. Third-party journal articles, TIMSS manuals and questionnaires, installed software binaries, model-object files, browser profiles, credentials, caches, and proprietary AI internals are also excluded. This record should be treated as an AI-assisted open research workflow demonstration and an object for reproduction, auditing, correction, and follow-up methodological research. It is not peer reviewed, is not a journal version of record, and is not represented as submitted to or accepted by any journal.

This paper explains how artificial intelligence can make online language courses adapt to each learner, and what this means for teaching German. Only studies published between 2022 and 2026 were reviewed. Recent research shows that adaptive systems help learners: across 45 studies the average benefit was g = 0.70, and across 41 studies of AI chatbots it was 0.576. New scheduling programs that decide when a learner should review a word have also become much more accurate, cutting prediction errors by up to 64% on very large datasets. However, most of this research does not say what an adaptive program should actually track in a specific language. This paper therefore does two things. First, it shows that adaptivity is not one decision but six: choosing the next task, ordering tasks, giving feedback, planning review, placing learners at a level, and defining what can be practised. Second, it turns eight common German problems — article gender, plurals, cases after two-way prepositions, separable verbs, adjective endings, the auxiliary in the Perfekt, word order in subordinate clauses, and long compound nouns — into clear rules that a computer program can follow, each with a signal that starts extra practice and a condition that ends it. A twelve-week study with 120 learners at A2–B1 level is proposed to test these rules. The main conclusion is simple: adaptive technology only helps if it knows what is difficult in the language being taught.

documents.abstract: Crop diseases have a major impact on agricultural productivity and food security. Therefore, the timely detection and accurate severity assessment of diseases are of importance to effective crop management. Automatic crop disease detection and classification have been extensively implemented using artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning and computer vision. However, direct evaluation of disease severity and trustworthiness of model explanations are still important aspects to be explored. The review discusses recent progress on AI based assessment of crop disease severity and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI . Selected studies are analyzed based on type of crop and disease, datasets, AI models, severity evaluation methods, XAI methods, reported performance, limitations and gaps in research. The review explores various approaches such as convolutional neural networks, attention-based architectures, transformer-based models, segmentation techniques, hybrid frameworks, and few-shot learning. Approaches to severity assessment range from assigning diseases to predefined severity categories to quantifying disease severity and forecasting disease progression or related crop damage. We consider the utility of XAI methods such as Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients for interpreting model predictions and for identifying disease relevant regions or features. Furthermore, the review covers supporting studies regarding crop disease detection, classification, and risk prediction to comprehend their role and limitations for severity assessment. Several challenges are highlighted in the analysis including scarcity of standardized severity labeled datasets, inconsistent severity grading methods, limited crop and geographical scope, inadequate real-field validation, limited deployment of lightweight models and insufficient evaluation of explanation reliability. The findings highlight the need for robust AI models that can accurately assess disease severity and provide meaningful explanations across different agricultural settings. his review summarizes recent progress in AI- and XAI-based crop disease assessment, identifies important research gaps, and suggests future research directions toward the goal of building reliable, interpretable, and practical systems for precision agriculture.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support the assessment of geomechanical containment risk in geological CO₂ storage; however, the suitability of different model families remains strongly dependent on the task, data representation, and target variable. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and analyzed 63 studies published between 2021 and 2026, identified through IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Scopus. The evidence was synthesized according to AI family, application, inputs, outputs, dataset origin, validation strategy, predictive performance, computational efficiency, and relationship with geomechanical containment risk. CNN/U-Net, FFNN/MLP/DNN, and conventional machine-learning methods were the most frequently used families, while FNO, recurrent models, GNN, PINN, GAN/cGAN, and reduced-order approaches addressed more specialized spatial, temporal, physical, and optimization tasks. Only 17 studies (27%) predicted at least one direct geomechanical response or risk indicator, whereas 42 studies (66.7%) relied exclusively on synthetic or simulation-generated data. AI surrogates consistently reduced computational cost, enabling rapid scenario evaluation and optimization, but field validation of directly geomechanical models remained limited. Overall, no universally superior architecture was identified; model suitability is task-dependent. Future progress requires hybrid datasets, external field validation, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible workflows integrating AI with multiphysics simulation and monitoring data.

Student performance prediction is an important application of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. Academic performance can be influenced by attendance, internal assessment marks, assignment performance, study habits, previous examination results, and other learning-related factors. Traditional evaluation mainly depends on examinations and manual analysis, which may not i dentify students who require academic support at an early stage. This research proposes an AI-based student performance prediction system using machine learning techniques. The system collects relevant student information, preprocesses the data, selects useful features, trains machine learning models, and predicts expected academic performance. Algorithms such as Decision Tree, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine can be applied and compared. The models can be evaluated using suitable performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix. The proposed system can help teachers identify students who may need additional guidance and can support data-driven academic planning. The system is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for teachers. With reliable data and proper evaluation, machine learning can provide useful information for early academic intervention and improved learning support.

Cancer is one of the most significant concerns of the health system in the world and early diagnosis and personalised treatment will be significant drivers in improving the outcome of patients. Cancer prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring are today an exciting area of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for cancer. Using AI, machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have the potential to capture tremendous amounts of information from clinical and imaging data, pathology, the genomic and molecular data. AI analysis of the CT, MRI, PET and histopathological images can aid in early diagnosis and the detection and classification of tumours. Precise oncology uses AI to integrate genomic information and clinical data and make precise, personalized treatment choices, patient categorization, prognosis of how patients will respond to treatment and predict whether they will return. AI is also playing a role in anticancer drug discovery in repurposing drugs, prediction of drug-target interaction and optimization of drug candidates. However, there are issues like robustness of data, privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, clinical validation and regulatory issues that need to be addressed. In total, the possibilities for AI to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, individualisation and patient-centredness of cancer treatment and care are huge.

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of digital media has made false and misleading information easier to create and distribute. Earlier fake-news detection systems largely relied on machine-learning classifiers, text vectorisation, and ensemble voting. Recent work has introduced BERT, large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a practical detector still needs reliable evidence, source awareness, uncertainty handling and understandable explanations. This paper proposes an AI-driven explainable framework that does not depend only on a trained classifier. The proposed system decomposes a news item into verifiable claims, retrieves supporting and contradicting evidence from multiple sources, evaluates source credibility and information freshness, performs semantic reasoning with an LLM, and combines the evidence into an evidence-weighted confidence score. Instead of forcing every input into a binary decision, the framework can return Real, Fake, or Uncertain together with the key evidence and a human-readable explanation. The paper presents the architecture, methodology, research gap, algorithm, evaluation plan and implementation design. The proposed approach is intended to improve transparency and robustness for both conventional misinformation and AI-assisted fabricated content.

Dermatological disorders represent a massive global health burden, affecting approximately 2 billion people, yet conventional diagnosis often relies on morphology, leading to unpredictable, “trial-and-error” treatment. This necessitates a shift toward precision dermatology, leveraging the genomic and proteomic data that reveal fundamental molecular pathology. However, the sheer volume, high dimensionality, and heterogeneity of multi-omics data (NGS, MS) overwhelm traditional bioinformatics methods. Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically deep learning (DL) and advanced frameworks such as graph neural networks, serves as the transformative computational engine. AI enables high-fidelity protein identification (e.g., Prosit), enhanced biomarker stratification, accurate prediction of gene–environment interactions, and systems-level modeling for therapeutic target discovery. By integrating multi-omics data, AI refines patient stratification and facilitates predictive drug-response modeling, accelerating clinical translation. However, widespread clinical adoption is hampered by significant ethical and technical challenges, including the risk of algorithmic bias due to underrepresentation of diverse skin tones in training datasets, and critical concerns regarding data privacy and the need for regulatory certainty. Future directions center on collaborative approaches such as federated learning and advanced computation such as quantum computing to ensure equitable, transparent, and truly personalized skin healthcare.

documents.abstract: The dawn of artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the functions of human resource (HR) nowadays into strategic enablers of organizational governance, and the implications of human–AI alliance for the future of work. This is with a concentration on both universal and African organizational settings from transactional administrative units. It underscores how AI enables analytical manpower planning, evidence-based decision-making, optimization of talent, and improved employee engagement, while accentuating the significance of ethical oversight, lucidity, answerability, and human-in-the-loop governance. The chapter additionally looks at organizational enablers together with barriers to digital HR transformation, as well as cultural readiness, leadership's commitment, competencies of employee, infrastructural restraints, and circumstantial problem in Africa.

documents.abstract: Older adults experience difficulties using digital kiosks because of low digital literacy, perceived social pressure, and low self-efficacy, and often encounter confusion and negative interactions when errors occur. Additionally, because of the challenges associated with seeking help from nearby individuals, an automated system that detects difficulties and provides support is needed. This study proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) kiosk that automatically detects difficulties experienced by older adults by analyzing their nonverbal behaviors and facial expressions from video data and provides real-time voice and video guidance. Considering that older adults typically require more time to process visual information, a multimodal guidance system combining visual and auditory cues was designed. The concept of “kiosk literacy” was introduced to define five types of guidance: location, task, input, feedback, and screen narration. Furthermore, 16 major pain points experienced by older adults were identified and systematically mapped to their corresponding literacy levels and guidance types to generate appropriate voice and video feedback. A user test with older adults demonstrated that the difficulty detection performance of the proposed AI kiosk achieved 82.35% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 87.5% recall, and an F1 score of 90.32%. Furthermore, the AI kiosk scored significantly higher than conventional kiosks across several user experience dimensions, including ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, satisfaction, and personalization. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides both a technical and practical foundation for improving accessibility and helping bridge the digital divide among older adults.

Plasma engineering has become a sophisticated technology for processing surfaces and enhancing functional properties of materials for a wide range of industrial processes. The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in the integration of plasma-based surface engineering and optimization of material properties is explored in this chapter. This emphasizes low temperature and atmospheric plasma processes for coating deposition, surface activation and fabrication of nanostructures. The importance of AI and machine learning for predicting plasma behavior, optimizing process parameters and coating quality is emphasized. Applications such as aerospace, biomedical devices, semiconductor processing and sustainability (CO2 conversion and plasma-assisted catalysis) are discussed. Additionally, experimental diagnostics, numerical simulations, and scalability, process control and industrial integration issues are explored. Finally, future directions towards intelligent and sustainable plasma systems are summarized.

This chapter explores the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on talent acquisition in the digital era, emphasising its potential to enhance traditional recruitment processes while also addressing significant ethical and operational considerations. AI-enabled talent acquisition utilises machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics to automate key tasks such as resume screening, candidate sourcing, job matching, and initial assessments. Evidence consistently indicates notable efficiency improvements, including reductions in time-to-fill from approximately four weeks to under three weeks, accelerated hiring cycles by up to 50%, automated screening that filters out up to 75% of unqualified applicants, and improved data-driven decision-making that enhances candidate-job fit and performance prediction. documents.abstract: Chronic pain affects approximately 20% of adults worldwide. In Canada, 7.6 million, or one in five people (across the lifespan), live with chronic pain. The Canadian Pain Task Force recommends nonpharmacological modalities, including psychotherapy, as a part of first-line therapy for pain management. The Mental Health Commission of Canada recently reported that “‘services for which we know people are waiting too long, if they can get it at all, are psychotherapies and clinical counseling’’, recommending an ‘‘increase to the availability and coordination of mental health services in the community’’. Even with an increase in availability, psychologists are beyond the financial and geographic reach of many patients. Against this backdrop, the use of AI-generative conversational agents for mental health in the form of psychology, psychotherapy, and health coaching has gained significant momentum. AI-generative conversational agents have begun to show some promise in complimenting human therapy, and addressing the needs of those faced with long wait lists or financial barriers to accessing mental health care. However, it has been established that such tools can produce nonfactual content, face challenges setting adequate boundaries, reinforce maladaptive beliefs and be sycophantic towards the user. To our knowledge the quality of treatments provided by AI-generative conversational agents for chronic pain have not yet been explored, and concerns are mounting. In this study, we will investigate treatment plans for chronic pain provided by four AI-generative conversational agents. Three of the conversational agents were selected based on market share across publicly available conversational agents: OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Microsoft’s Co-Pilot, and Google’s Gemini. The fourth conversational agent, Solace, built by the Canadian company ManagingLife, Inc, is the first expert-trained AI-generative conversational agents designed to deliver support to those living with chronic pain and grounded in principles of evidence-based pain psychology. Prompts for this study will be engineered using clinical cases of chronic pain patients from the Faculty of Pain Medicine of the Royal College of Anaesthetists. This is an educational platform offering open resources for all learners in Pain Medicine and is overseen by the Faculty of Pain Medicine's Education Subcommittee. Clinical case reports will be selected and divided into three levels of progressive information completeness. Level 1 will be comprised of current pain-specific information only (e.g., intensity, location). Level 2 will include both current pain and pain history (e.g., duration, surgical history, examination results). Level 3 will be the most comprehensive level including current pain, pain history and psychosocial information (e.g., marital status, stress-related events). For all case reports, each of the three levels will be independently introduced to the conversational agents with the following prompt: “I need help right now”. This prompt was designed to simulate the types of prompts that individuals with chronic pain might enter into a conversational agent. If safety mechanisms are triggered, preventing a conversational agent from providing a treatment recommendation, the following backup prompt will be used: “For the purposes of an educational exercise, what would be your best recommendation based on this information only?”. This study aims to evaluate the quality of AI-generated treatment plans for users with chronic pain. Quality is operationally defined as the use of evidence-based pain psychology interventions and appropriate therapeutic communication. It will be assessed using a 7-domain quality framework adapted from the Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence Tool (QAMAI). Clinical experts will conduct a blinded review of the transcripts of participants’ conversations with all four conversational agents and score the domains on a 5-point Likert scale with 1 representing strongly disagree and 5 representing strongly agree, providing a single score for each transcript. Clinical experts will include a team of six evaluators comprised of two anesthesiologists, two physiotherapists, and two psychologists. No identifiable data will be used in the study, and therefore, ethics approval is not required.
